title: The Master of Arms
body:
The Master of Arms

एकं लक्ष्यं समाधाय मनः संयम्य योगतः।
शरं मुञ्चति यो धीरः स वै सिद्धिमवाप्नुयात्॥

"Fixing his focus upon a single target, subduing the mind through the discipline of yoga, the brave warrior who releases his shaft with absolute precision will certainly attain supreme perfection."

Drona entered Hastinapur in quiet disguise, staying in the humble residence of his brother-in-law Kripacharya. One afternoon, the young Kuru princes—both the sons of Dhritarashtra and the sons of Pandu—were playing with a ball on the outskirts of the capital. In the course of their competitive play, the ball bounced away and plunged into a deep, steep well. In their anxious efforts to peer into the dark well, Yudhishthira's royal signet ring also slipped from his finger and fell into the clear, distant water. The princes gathered around the well in complete helplessness, seeing the ring and the ball shining from the bottom but finding no physical mechanism to reach them.
A dark-complexioned Brahmana of magnetic presence stood nearby, watching their anxiety with a gentle smile. 'Princes of the Bharata line,' he spoke, 'how is it that you, trained in the royal arts, cannot retrieve a ball from a well? Watch closely, and I shall do it for you.' Drona took a simple blade of grass and, reciting secret words of power (mantras) to propel it as an arrow, sent it into the well. The blade of grass sped down and transfixed itself into the core of the ball. He then released another blade of grass, which stuck seamlessly to the tail of the first. In rapid succession, he built an unbreakable chain of grass blades, with which he calmly pulled the ball out to the surface. He then borrowed a bow, fixed an arrow, and shot it directly through the center of the submerged ring, the rebounding arrow bringing the ring back into the hand of the stunned Yudhishthira.
The princes bowed down in reverence, asking who this extraordinary master was. Drona smiled and said: 'Go to Bhishma and describe these deeds; he will tell you who I am.' When Bheeshma heard of the chain of grass blades, he immediately recognized the arrival of Bharadwaja's son. He brought Drona to the palace with royal honors, installing him as the supreme preceptor (Acharya) of the royal household. This episode is rich in spiritual symbolism. The deep well is the dark pit of material existence (Samsara), and the lost ball and ring are the Jivatma's lost connection with the Divine. The fragile blades of grass, when energized by the sacred mantra, represent the subtle disciplines of spiritual practice (Sadhana). On their own, they are weak, but when joined in a continuous, uninterrupted chain of devotion, they can lift the soul out of the deepest abyss of ignorance.
